settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: sizeMax and fileSizeMax exist (FileUploadBase.java:161,167) and are enforced via LimitedInputStream when set to >= 0 (FileUploadBase.java:963-981, 770-797), which can indirectly cap total request bytes.
The documented streaming API intentionally processes data under constant memory (MultipartStream.java:34-38, per-part streaming), so each part does not necessarily buffer fully in memory.
candidates.description: FileItemIteratorImpl.findNextItem() iterates and yields each multipart part in an unbounded for(;;) loop; there is no counter or maximum-part check anywhere in the reviewed code. ProgressNotifier.noteItem() increments an items counter, but it is only passed to a ProgressListener (MultipartStream.java:142-153) and is never used to reject or stop parsing. Consequently a request containing a very large number of parts (each possibly tiny) is parsed and materialized without an upper bound, allowing resource-exhaustion/DoS. The class only exposes sizeMax (total request size) and fileSizeMax (per-file size), both defaulting to -1 (unlimited), so unless an application explicitly sets a size cap, neither the part count nor aggregate processing is bounded.
missing_evidence: Whether a higher-level container (servlet) applies its own request-size limit by default is not determinable from these spans.
The exact resource cost per part (header buffer, object allocation, listener callbacks) was not measured.
MultipartStream.readBoundary/skipPreamble internals were not in the inspected spans, so per-part overhead is not fully traced.
preconditions: Application accepts multipart/form-data requests via getItemIterator/parseRequest without setting sizeMax.
Attacker can send a multipart body with a very large number of parts.
candidates.title: No limit on number of multipart parts processed (unbounded part count DoS)
